items.title: The Post-Mauryan Period & Political Landscape
items.body:
## Between the Mauryas and the Guptas

- The **Post-Mauryan period (2nd century BCE – 3rd century AD)** is the interval between the **fall of the Mauryan Empire** and the **rise of the Gupta Empire**.
- The Mauryan Empire **disintegrated after Ashoka's death** due to **weak successors**; provinces began **declaring independence** as central authority weakened.
- It saw the rise of **regional kingdoms — the Shungas, Kanvas and Chedis** — alongside invasions by **Central Asian tribes** (Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians and Kushanas).
- **Kalinga declared independence**, while the **Satavahanas** gained control of southern India; the **north-west** fell under successive foreign invaders.
- The **Shungas, followers of Brahmanism**, replaced the Mauryas and opposed the Buddhist policies of their predecessors.
keyPoints: Post-Mauryan period spans the 2nd century BCE to 3rd century AD — between the Mauryan fall and the Gupta rise.
The Mauryan Empire disintegrated after Ashoka's death because of weak successors and provinces breaking away.
Regional powers emerged: Shungas, Kanvas, Chedis; Satavahanas took the south and Kalinga became independent.
Central Asian tribes — Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas — invaded the north-west.
The Shungas were Brahmanical rulers who reacted against Mauryan Buddhist policy.
items.mnemonic: Three post-Mauryan Indian dynasties = 'SKC' → Shunga → Kanva → Chedi.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Post-Mauryan Period; Political Developments)

items.title: Pushyamitra Shunga & the Founding of the Shunga Dynasty
items.body:
## Foundation of the Shunga Dynasty (185 BCE – 73 BCE)

- **Pushyamitra Shunga**, a **general of the Mauryas**, **assassinated the last Mauryan king Brihadratha** and established the **Shunga dynasty** in **185 BCE**.
- Capitals were **Pataliputra and Vidisha**; the territory covered **central and northern India up to the Narmada River**.
- Shunga rulers controlled **north-central India**, **resisting Indo-Greek invasions** and protecting the **Gangetic Valley** from external forces.

## Pushyamitra Shunga (185 BCE – 149 BCE)

- Performed **two Ashvamedha Yagnas** to assert his legitimacy (recorded in the **Ayodhya Inscription**).
- Defended against **Indo-Greek invasions** and **Kharavela of Kalinga**.
- Despite his adherence to Brahmanism, he **renovated the Bharhut Stupa**.
- He is mentioned in **Banabhatta's Harshacharita**.

figure.alt: Map of the Sunga Empire around 185 BCE showing territory up to the Narmada with Pataliputra, Vidisa, Bharhut and Saketa, bordered by the Greco-Bactrian and Satavahana realms
figure.caption: The Sunga Empire (c. 185 BCE) reached central-northern India up to the Narmada, with Pataliputra and Vidisa as centres and Bharhut within its territory.

keyPoints: Pushyamitra Shunga, a Mauryan general, killed the last Mauryan king Brihadratha and founded the Shunga dynasty in 185 BCE.
Shunga capitals were Pataliputra and Vidisha; territory extended to the Narmada River.
Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha Yagnas (Ayodhya Inscription) to assert legitimacy.
He resisted Indo-Greek invasions and Kharavela of Kalinga while protecting the Gangetic Valley.
Though a Brahmanist, he renovated the Bharhut Stupa; he is mentioned in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.
items.mnemonic: Pushyamitra 'PB': Pushyamitra killed Brihadratha — and did two aShvamedhas ('Shunga').
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Shunga Dynasty; Pushyamitra Shunga)

items.title: Key Rulers of the Shunga Dynasty
items.body:
## Successors of Pushyamitra

- **Agnimitra Shunga (149 BCE – 141 BCE)** — his reign is known through **Kalidasa's play Malvikagnimitra**, which describes his romance with **Princess Malvika**; he **suppressed rebellions in Vidarbha**.
- **Vasumitra** — defended against **Indo-Greek invasions**.
- **Bhagabhadra** — associated with the **Heliodorus Pillar** near **Vidisha**, dedicated by a **Greek ambassador to Vasudeva (Krishna)** — evidence of Bhagavatism attracting even Greeks.
- **Devabhuti**, the **last Shunga ruler**, was **assassinated by Vasudeva Kanva**, ending the dynasty.
keyPoints: Agnimitra (149–141 BCE) features in Kalidasa's Malvikagnimitra and suppressed Vidarbha rebellions.
Vasumitra defended the dynasty against Indo-Greek invasions.
Bhagabhadra is linked to the Heliodorus Pillar near Vidisha, dedicated by a Greek envoy to Vasudeva Krishna.
Devabhuti was the last Shunga ruler.
Devabhuti's assassination by Vasudeva Kanva ended the Shunga dynasty.
Agnimitra, son of Pushyamitra, is the hero of Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitra.
items.mnemonic: Heliodorus Pillar = a Greek bowing to Krishna — foreign devotion to Vasudeva under Bhagabhadra.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Key Rulers of the Shunga Dynasty)

items.title: The Kanva Dynasty (73 BCE – 28 BCE)
items.body:
## Vasudeva Kanva Founds the Dynasty

- **Vasudeva Kanva**, a **Brahmin minister of the Shunga king**, **killed Devabhuti** and established the **Kanva dynasty** in **73 BCE**, with capitals at **Pataliputra and Vidisha**.
- The Kanvas maintained **Brahmanical traditions**, performed **Vedic rituals**, and ruled much of the **Gangetic plain**, retaining Shunga administrative structures for continuity.

## Key Rulers

- **Bhumimitra** — Vasudeva's successor; **coins bearing his name** found in the **Panchala region** attest his control there.
- **Narayana** — tried to hold the dynasty's power against growing challenges.
- **Susharman** — the **last Kanva ruler**, **overthrown by the Satavahanas**, ending the dynasty and ushering in Satavahana rule.

figure.alt: Map of India in the 1st century BCE showing Magadha under the Kanva Dynasty flanked by the Satavahana Empire, Indo-Scythian kingdoms and Kalinga
figure.caption: The Kanva dynasty ruled Magadha and the Gangetic plain, bordered by the Satavahanas to the south and Indo-Scythians to the north-west.

keyPoints: Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin Shunga minister, killed Devabhuti and founded the Kanva dynasty in 73 BCE.
Kanva capitals were Pataliputra and Vidisha; they upheld Brahmanical traditions and Vedic rituals.
Bhumimitra succeeded Vasudeva; coins of his found in Panchala show his control there.
Narayana struggled to hold power amid mounting challenges.
Susharman, the last Kanva ruler, was overthrown by the Satavahanas.
items.mnemonic: Kanva line 'VBNS' → Vasudeva → Bhumimitra → Narayana → Susharman (ends at Satavahanas).

items.title: The Chedi (Mahameghavahana) Dynasty & Kharavela
items.body:
## Chedi Dynasty of Kalinga (1st Century BCE)

- The **Chedi Dynasty**, also called the **Mahameghavahana Dynasty**, emerged in **Kalinga** after Mauryan decline; it was **founded by King Abhichandra** with capital at **Suktimati-Puri** (on the Suktimati River).

## King Kharavela — the Great Chedi Ruler

- **Kharavela** was a **Jain ruler** known for his **military conquests** and **religious patronage**.
- His achievements are recorded in the **Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi script)**, located in the **Udayagiri hills**.
- He launched **campaigns against the Satavahanas** and **expanded his territory**.
- He constructed the **Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves** as **residences for Jain monks**.
- His son **Kudepasiri** is mentioned in the **Mancapuri Cave Inscription**.
keyPoints: The Chedi (Mahameghavahana) dynasty rose in Kalinga; founded by Abhichandra with capital Suktimati-Puri.
Kharavela was a Jain ruler famed for conquests and religious patronage.
His deeds are recorded in the Hathigumpha Inscription (Brahmi script) in the Udayagiri hills.
He campaigned against the Satavahanas and built the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves for Jain monks.
His son Kudepasiri appears in the Mancapuri Cave Inscription.
items.mnemonic: Kharavela = 'Jain King of the Elephant Cave' — Hathigumpha ('elephant cave') records his Kalinga deeds.

items.title: Stupas & Buddhist Architecture (Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati)
items.body:
## Great Stupas of the Post-Mauryan Age

- **Sanchi Stupa (Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh)** — originally built by **Ashoka** and **expanded by the Shungas**; famous for **elaborate Toranas (gateways)** and **Jataka tales** on the gateways; located on the **Dakshinapatha** trade route.
- **Bharhut Stupa (Satna, Madhya Pradesh)** — **discovered by Alexander Cunningham**; noted for **red stone railings** and **narrative reliefs**, depicting **Queen Mayadevi's dream** and the **Ruru Jataka**.
- **Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh)** — known for **intricate carvings**, **Buddhist narratives**, **floral motifs** and **life scenes of the Buddha**.

## Dynastic Contributions

- The **Shungas** promoted Brahmanism yet **renovated Buddhist monuments** like the Sanchi and Bharhut stupas and introduced **decorated toranas**.
- The **Kanvas** continued Brahmanical temple construction, following Shunga artistic traditions.

figure.alt: The Great Stupa at Sanchi with its hemispherical dome, railing and elaborately carved torana gateway against a blue sky
figure.caption: The Great Stupa at Sanchi — begun by Ashoka and expanded by the Shungas, famous for its carved toranas depicting Jataka tales.

keyPoints: Sanchi Stupa (Vidisha) was begun by Ashoka and expanded by the Shungas; known for toranas and Jataka scenes on the Dakshinapatha route.
Bharhut Stupa (Satna) was discovered by Alexander Cunningham; noted for red stone railings and reliefs of Mayadevi's dream and the Ruru Jataka.
Amaravati Stupa (Andhra Pradesh) is known for intricate carvings, floral motifs and scenes from the Buddha's life.
The Shungas renovated Buddhist stupas and introduced decorated toranas despite promoting Brahmanism.
The Kanvas continued Brahmanical temple construction in the Shunga artistic tradition.
items.mnemonic: Stupa trio 'SBA' → Sanchi (toranas) · Bharhut (Cunningham, red railings) · Amaravati (marble narratives).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Art and Architecture; Stupas; Contribution of Various Dynasties)

items.title: Rock-cut Architecture & Schools of Sculpture
items.body:
## Rock-cut Architecture

- **Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves (Odisha)** — built under **King Kharavela**; house the **Hathigumpha inscription** in Brahmi script and the double-storey **Ranigumpha Cave** with exquisite sculptures.
- **Ajanta Caves (Maharashtra)** — early **Hinayana** caves with simple architecture, later **Mahayana** caves with Buddha sculptures and paintings depicting **Jataka tales and royal processions**.

## Schools of Sculpture

- **Mathura School (Uttar Pradesh)** — **red sandstone** sculptures; produced **early Buddha statues** and **Jain Tirthankara** images with stylised features.
- **Gandhara School (North-West India, Pakistan)** — influenced by **Greek and Roman art**; used **grey schist stone** to create realistic Buddha images with **Greek-style drapery and curly hair**.
- **Amaravati School (Andhra Pradesh)** — **white marble** sculptures depicting Buddhist narratives and floral motifs with high detailing.
keyPoints: Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves (Odisha) were built under Kharavela and hold the Hathigumpha inscription and the double-storey Ranigumpha cave.
Ajanta caves (Maharashtra) progress from simple Hinayana to Mahayana caves with Buddha sculptures and Jataka paintings.
Mathura School used red sandstone for early Buddha and Jain Tirthankara images.
Gandhara School used grey schist and Greco-Roman influence for realistic Buddhas with Greek drapery and curly hair.
Amaravati School used white marble for detailed Buddhist narratives and floral motifs.
items.mnemonic: Sculpture stones: Mathura = red sandstone, Gandhara = grey schist, Amaravati = white marble (R-G-W).

items.title: Patanjali, the Mahabhashya & Language
items.body:
## Revival of Sanskrit Learning

- **Sanskrit gained prominence** in the post-Mauryan age, becoming the language of **religious and literary texts**.
- **Patanjali** authored the **Mahabhashya** on **Sanskrit grammar** and the **Yoga Sutras** on **yoga philosophy** — Patanjali is traditionally linked to the Shunga court of Pushyamitra.
- The **Brahmi script** evolved further, with connections to the **Kalinga Brahmi** and **Maurya scripts** — the same Brahmi in which Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription was engraved.
keyPoints: Sanskrit became the dominant language of religious and literary texts in the post-Mauryan period.
Patanjali authored the Mahabhashya on Sanskrit grammar.
Patanjali also wrote the Yoga Sutras on yoga philosophy.
The Brahmi script evolved further, connected to the Kalinga Brahmi and Maurya scripts.
Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is itself in the Brahmi script.
items.mnemonic: Patanjali = two great works — 'grammar + yoga' → Mahabhashya (language) and Yoga Sutras (mind).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan (Language and Literature)

items.title: Religion & Society in the Post-Mauryan Period
items.body:
## Brahmanical Revival

- **Brahmanism regained prominence** under the **Shunga dynasty**, reviving **Vedic rituals** such as the **Ashvamedha Yagna**.
- The **Varna system became rigid**, reinforcing the social hierarchy; **priests and rulers dominated society**, while **Shudras faced continued discrimination**.
- **Women's roles were restricted to domestic duties**, as prescribed in the **Manusmriti**.
- **Mixed castes emerged** as foreigners (Greeks, Shakas and others) integrated into Indian society.
keyPoints: Brahmanism revived under the Shungas, reviving Vedic rituals such as the Ashvamedha Yagna.
The Varna system became rigid, reinforcing social hierarchy.
Priests and rulers dominated society while Shudras faced continued discrimination.
Women's roles were restricted to domestic duties as prescribed in the Manusmriti.
Mixed castes emerged as foreigners integrated into Indian society.
items.mnemonic: Shunga society = 'rigid Varna + Manusmriti' — Brahmanical revival hardens the hierarchy.

items.title: Trade & Commerce in the Post-Mauryan Period
items.body:
## Flourishing Trade Networks

- **Merchant guilds and trading corporations** flourished during this period.
- **Mathura** was known for producing **shataka cloth**.
- **Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha** were the **major trade routes** connecting different regions of the subcontinent.
- **Monsoon winds facilitated maritime trade** with **Rome and Southeast Asia**, enhancing commerce.
keyPoints: Merchant guilds and trading corporations flourished in the post-Mauryan economy.
Mathura was famous for producing shataka cloth.
Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha were the two major trade routes.
Monsoon winds enabled maritime trade with Rome and Southeast Asia.
Growing commerce linked the subcontinent to distant overseas markets.
items.mnemonic: Two great routes = 'U & D' — Uttarapatha (north) and Dakshinapatha (south).
